A political commentator might appear on a news channel after an election and explain: "Here is why this result happened, what it signals about the country, and what we should expect next."

A few things define a commentator:

  • They have an audience. A commentator speaks or writes for people — viewers, readers, or listeners. Without an audience, there is no commentary.
  • They interpret, not just describe. Anyone can say "it rained heavily today." A commentator says "this is the worst flooding the region has seen in a decade, and here's why it was predictable."
  • They have some level of authority or knowledge. People trust commentators because they are seen as informed — either from experience, expertise, or careful observation.
  • They can express opinions. Unlike a neutral journalist, commentators are generally expected to share a point of view. Their commentary is colored by their analysis and judgment.

The word "commentator" appears across many domains:

  • Sports: "The cricket commentator kept the audience engaged through a slow over."
  • Politics and news: "She is a well-known political commentator who appears regularly on television."
  • Literature and academia: A scholar who writes detailed notes and explanations about a book or ancient text can also be called a commentator. (Example: "Medieval commentators wrote extensively on Aristotle's works.")
  • Social media and online spaces: Today, the word is also used loosely for people who regularly share opinions online — bloggers, YouTubers, podcasters — though this usage is more informal.

It helps to know how "commentator" differs from words that seem close to it:

  • Reporter / Journalist: Reports facts, aims to be neutral and objective. A commentator goes further by adding analysis and opinion.
  • Narrator: Describes a sequence of events (like in a film or documentary) without necessarily analyzing them. A commentator actively interprets and evaluates.
  • Analyst: Very similar to a commentator, but "analyst" often implies a more data-driven, technical, or neutral approach. A commentator can be more opinionated and expressive.
  • Critic: Focuses specifically on evaluating the quality of something (a film, a book, a performance). A commentator has a wider scope — they may analyze, explain, or evaluate, but they are not limited to judgment of quality.

A commentator is a person who observes events or issues and communicates their description, explanation, or opinion about them to an audience — whether live during a sports match, or through media when discussing news and public affairs.
3060: Commerce is the large-scale, organized activity of buying and selling goods and services. It is the engine that keeps an economy moving — every time a product is made, transported, purchased, or exchanged for money, commerce is happening.

Commerce is about exchange. One party has something valuable — a product, raw material, or service — and another party wants it and is willing to pay for it. Commerce is the entire system through which these exchanges happen, repeatedly and at scale, across businesses, cities, and countries.

A single neighbor selling a bicycle to another neighbor is just a transaction. Commerce is bigger — it refers to the ongoing, systematic flow of buying and selling that runs through an entire economy.

Commerce deals in two things:

Goods — physical, tangible products: wheat, clothing, steel, medicine, electronics, furniture, oil, machinery.

Services — intangible offerings that someone provides for payment: banking, shipping, insurance, legal advice, advertising, consulting, software.

A farmer selling grain to a flour mill is commerce. A shipping company transporting goods across the country is commerce. A bank lending money to a business so it can grow is commerce.

Commerce can happen at different scales:

Local commerce — a bakery buying flour from a local supplier, or a shop sourcing goods from nearby manufacturers.

National commerce — a large retailer distributing products to stores across an entire country.

International commerce — countries buying and selling with one another: importing oil, exporting cars, outsourcing software development. When commerce crosses national borders, it is often called trade or international trade.

The bigger the scale, the more complex the systems needed to support it.

Commerce is never just about two parties exchanging money for goods. Supporting it is an entire ecosystem:

Banking and finance — businesses need loans, payment processing, and accounts to manage money.

Transportation and logistics — goods need to physically move from producers to buyers, across roads, railways, ships, and air routes.

Communication — buyers and sellers need to find each other, negotiate, and confirm deals.

Law and contracts — agreements need to be enforceable, and disputes need resolution.

Government and regulation — rules that prevent fraud, set standards, protect consumers, and ensure fair competition.

All of this together forms what we call the commercial infrastructure of a society. Commerce cannot function without it.

Retail commerce — selling goods or services directly to the end consumer. A supermarket, a pharmacy, an online store — all retail.

Wholesale commerce — selling goods in large quantities, not to ordinary consumers, but to businesses that will then resell them. A food distributor supplying restaurants is a wholesaler.

E-commerce — buying and selling conducted entirely over the internet. Online shopping, digital subscriptions, app-based services — all forms of e-commerce.

International commerce / trade — the exchange of goods and services across national borders. A country importing semiconductors and exporting agricultural products is engaging in international commerce.
How Commerce Differs From Similar Words

These words are closely related and often confused:

Trade is nearly synonymous with commerce, but tends to focus more on the direct act of exchanging goods (especially between countries). Commerce is slightly broader — it includes not just the exchange but all the surrounding activity (finance, logistics, communication) that makes the exchange possible.

Business refers to individual companies or enterprises — the participants in commerce. A business is an actor within the commercial system.

Industry refers to the production side of the economy — manufacturing, mining, farming. Commerce is more about the distribution and exchange side, though the two are deeply connected.

Economy is the broadest term of all — it covers everything: production, distribution, consumption. Commerce is one major part of the economy.

Commerce is what allows specialization. Without it, every person or community would have to produce everything they need on their own — grow their own food, make their own tools, generate their own electricity. Commerce allows a farmer to grow food, an engineer to build machines, and a programmer to write software — and then exchange the results of their work for everything else they need.

This specialization driven by commerce is the primary reason living standards rise over time. It also connects nations economically. Countries that trade with each other develop shared interests, which creates stability and cooperation.

Commerce is present in nearly every part of modern life, even when it is invisible:

When you buy groceries, you are participating in retail commerce. When a factory orders raw materials from a supplier, that is business-to-business commerce. When your country buys oil from abroad and sells software services in return, that is international commerce. When a bank transfers money between two companies, it is facilitating commerce.

The roads, ports, internet networks, payment systems, laws, and institutions that surround all of this activity are the infrastructure of commerce — the things that make all of it possible.

Commerce, as a noun, means the entire system of organized, large-scale buying and selling of goods and services — including the financial, logistical, legal, and communication networks that make such exchange possible. It operates at every scale, from a local market to global trade, and is the foundation on which modern economies and societies are built.
3061: Commercial describes anything that is connected to or driven by commerce — the activity of buying and selling goods or services to earn money. Think of commerce as trade and business for profit. Whenever you see the word "commercial," ask yourself: Is this thing related to business, trade, or making money? If yes, "commercial" is likely the right word.

1. Related to trade and business in general

The most basic use: something is "commercial" simply because it belongs to the world of business and trade.

  • Commercial law = the body of law that governs business transactions, contracts, and trade
  • Commercial bank = a bank that handles everyday business and financial transactions (lending money, accepting deposits) for individuals and companies — as opposed to, say, a central bank
  • Commercial ties between countries = the trading and business relationships between nations

Here, "commercial" is neutral — it just means "of or relating to business/trade."

2. Done with the primary goal of making profit

This is perhaps the most commonly encountered meaning. When something is designed, created, or done mainly to generate money — rather than for art, science, charity, or personal use — it is called commercial.

  • A commercial farm grows crops or raises animals specifically to sell them in the market for profit, not just to feed the farmer's family.
  • A commercial film is made with the intention of being a box-office success — that is, to earn as much money as possible.
  • A commercial product is something manufactured and sold to the public for a price.

The emphasis here is on profit as the driving force.

3. Designed for business/professional/large-scale use

"Commercial" can describe things that are built or meant for use in a business environment — usually bigger, more powerful, or more durable than what an ordinary person would use at home.

  • A commercial kitchen is the kind of large, professionally equipped kitchen found in a restaurant, not a home. It can handle cooking large quantities of food at high speed.
  • A commercial vehicle is a truck, van, or bus used to transport goods or passengers as part of a business operation — not a personal car.
  • Commercial real estate (or commercial property) refers to buildings and land used for business purposes — offices, shops, warehouses, hotels — as opposed to residential property where people live.
  • Commercial aviation refers to the airline industry — companies like Air India or Emirates that fly passengers and cargo for money.

The contrast here is: commercial use vs. personal/home/residential use.

4. Available to the general public through normal market channels

Something "commercial" is on the market — you can buy or access it through ordinary, public means. This distinguishes it from things that are experimental, restricted, classified, or specially developed.

  • A commercial flight is a regular scheduled flight that anyone can book a ticket for. A military flight or a private charter is not "commercial."
  • Commercial software is software you can purchase or download from the market. Before it is released publicly, it might exist only as a prototype.
  • Commercial availability of a drug means it is approved, produced, and sold in pharmacies for general use.

5. Relating to advertising

You will often encounter "commercial" in the context of media and advertising.

  • A commercial break on television or radio is the pause in programming when advertisements are shown.
  • Commercial content is content created to promote or advertise a product or service.

This use comes from the idea that advertising is how businesses reach customers — it is a tool of commerce. In informal speech, people often use "commercial" as a noun to mean a single advertisement (e.g., "I saw a funny commercial on TV"), but in its adjective form, it means pertaining to advertisements or the commercial activity of promoting something.
The Subtle Connotation: When "Commercial" Has a Slightly Negative Tone

Here is something important that most learners miss. In many contexts, particularly in art, music, literature, and film, calling something "commercial" carries a mildly critical or dismissive tone. It implies that the work was made to sell rather than to be genuinely creative, meaningful, or authentic.

  • "That band sold out — their new album is too commercial." (It sounds like it was made just to be popular and sell well, not out of artistic integrity.)
  • "The novel is well-written but very commercial." (It's the kind of book written to appeal to the widest possible audience and make money — easy, entertaining, not challenging.)
  • "The film had a commercial feel to it." (It seemed factory-produced, safe, and crowd-pleasing rather than original or thoughtful.)

So in these contexts, "commercial" can quietly suggest: mass-produced, profit-driven, lacking depth or originality. This is not always the intended meaning — context is everything — but it is a common undercurrent.

On the flip side, calling something a commercial success is entirely positive: it means something sold very well or made a lot of money.

Here are important phrases where "commercial" appears, with brief explanations:

  • Commercial success — how well something did in terms of sales or profit ("The product was a commercial success.")
  • Commercial viability — whether something is capable of making money or surviving as a business ("The startup lacks commercial viability.")
  • Commercial use — using something for business or profit-making purposes, as opposed to personal or non-profit use (important in copyright and licensing)
  • Commercial district — an area of a city dominated by shops, offices, and businesses (as opposed to a residential neighbourhood)
  • Commercial interests — the financial and business motivations behind a decision or action
  • Commercial appeal — the quality of attracting many buyers or a wide audience ("The design has strong commercial appeal.")
  • Non-commercial — the direct opposite: not done for profit; for personal, educational, or charitable purposes

If you had to remember just one thing: Commercial = related to or driven by buying, selling, and making money. Everything else — the large-scale kitchens, the TV ad breaks, the profit-first films, the public airlines — flows from this central idea.
3062:
To commiserate means to express sympathy and share in someone's sorrow, disappointment, or bad luck — often in a mutual, back-and-forth way.

Think of it as saying "I feel your pain, and I'm here with you in it."

Here is what makes this word special and slightly different from simply "feeling sorry" for someone:

Commiserating is active and shared. It is not just a quiet internal feeling of sympathy. It is something you do — usually out loud, and usually together with the other person. Both people often lean into the sadness or frustration, almost like bonding over it.

A good mental image: Two colleagues sitting together after a project got cancelled, sighing, venting, and telling each other "I know, I know, it's awful" — that is commiserating.
How It's Used in a Sentence

The verb almost always appears with these two patterns:

1. Commiserate with someone
→ You are expressing sympathy toward that person.

  • She called her best friend to commiserate with her after the breakup.
  • He commiserated with his teammate after they lost the final match.

2. Commiserate about / over something
→ You and the other person are sharing sorrow about a particular thing.

  • They sat together commiserating about how terrible the weather had been all week.
  • The two friends met for coffee to commiserate over their job rejections.

These two patterns are also often combined:

  • I commiserated with my neighbour over the endless construction noise on our street.
Everyday Examples to Make It Stick

Example 1 — Relatable and casual:
You and your coworker both had a horrible Monday. The meetings were pointless, the coffee machine broke, and your boss was in a bad mood. At the end of the day, you both sit down and say to each other, "What a disaster of a day, right?" and spend ten minutes venting together.
→ You are commiserating with each other.

Example 2 — Sports:
Two fans whose team just lost a big game stand outside the stadium, shaking their heads, groaning, and saying "I can't believe that happened."
→ They are commiserating over the loss.

Example 3 — More serious:
A man just found out his business deal fell through after months of work. His close friend, who knows how hard he worked for it, sits with him and says "That is genuinely awful. I'm so sorry. You deserved better."
→ The friend is commiserating with him.

1. Feeling vs. Expressing

You can feel sympathy silently in your heart. But commiserating requires you to show it — through words, presence, or tone. It is an outward act.

2. It Often Goes Both Ways

Commiserating has a mutual, conversational quality. Both people are often in it together — sharing, venting, nodding along. It is less like a speech and more like a dialogue of shared sadness.

3. It Is Not About Fixing Anything

This is a key point. When you commiserate with someone, you are not trying to solve their problem or cheer them up. You are simply acknowledging their pain and sitting with them in it. The purpose is emotional solidarity, not solutions.

4. The Scale of Misfortune

Commiserate is most naturally used for disappointments, setbacks, frustrations, and bad luck — things that are genuinely upsetting but not necessarily catastrophic. Missing a flight, losing a game, getting a bad grade, a plan falling apart, a hard week at work — these are the everyday territories of commiseration. For extremely grave tragedies (like a death in the family), people more commonly use words like grieve or mourn together. Though commiserate can be used for serious situations, it has a somewhat everyday, conversational feel to it.
How It Differs From Similar Words

What it meansKey difference
SympathizeTo understand and care about someone's sufferingMore general; doesn't necessarily imply a shared conversation or mutual venting
EmpathizeTo deeply feel what another person feels, as if you are in their shoesMore about internal emotional understanding than expressing it
ConsoleTo comfort someone and try to ease their painThe goal is to lift them up; commiseration does not try to fix the feeling
CommiserateTo express shared sorrow with someone, often mutually and conversationallyHas a bonding, "we're in this together" quality; neither person is trying to fix it

The simplest way to remember the difference:

  • A consoler says: "Don't worry, it will get better."
  • A commiserator says: "I know. It's awful. I feel it too."

There is something genuinely warm and human about commiserating. It tells the other person: "You are not alone in this. I see your pain, I acknowledge it, and I am here beside you." It does not demand that anyone be strong or move on quickly. It simply allows two people to sit together in their shared frustration or sorrow — and that, in itself, can be a great comfort.

To commiserate = to express sympathy and share in someone's sorrow or disappointment, usually in a mutual, spoken, and heartfelt way — without trying to fix the problem, just to say: "I feel this with you."
3063: Commiseration is the act of expressing sympathy and sharing in someone else's sorrow, grief, or disappointment. When you offer commiseration to someone, you are essentially saying, "I feel sorry about what happened to you, and I share in your sadness."

Think of it this way. When something bad happens to a person — they lose a competition, they fail an exam, they don't get a job they really wanted, or they go through any kind of setback — they feel pain, disappointment, or sadness. Commiseration is the warm, human act of sitting with that person in their pain, emotionally speaking. It is about letting someone know that their suffering is seen, understood, and felt by you too.

The word almost always involves two parties: the person who is suffering, and the person who is offering commiseration. It is a deeply relational word — it is something you offer to someone or share with someone.
What It Looks Like in Real Life

Commiseration can take many forms. It can be a hug. It can be a few kind words: "I'm so sorry that happened to you. You deserved better." It can be two colleagues quietly shaking their heads together after a project got rejected. It can be friends gathering after a sports team they all support loses an important match, and they sit together and say, "Well, that was painful."

The important thing to understand is that commiseration is not about solving the problem. It is not advice. It is not cheerful encouragement like, "Don't worry, you'll do better next time!" It is gentler and quieter than that. It is simply the act of acknowledging pain and saying, in effect, "Yes, this is hard, and I am sorry."
How the Word Is Used in Sentences

Here are some natural examples to show how the word works:

  • She offered her commiseration to her colleague who had been passed over for the promotion.
  • After losing the championship, the players looked to each other for commiseration.
  • He called his friend not to give advice, but simply to offer commiseration after the difficult week she'd had.
  • There was a moment of quiet commiseration between the two of them when they heard the news.

You will also frequently see the plural form: "commiserations." This is used as a direct expression of sympathy, much like saying "condolences" or "I'm sorry for your loss." For example: "Commiserations on not getting that scholarship — you worked so hard for it."

Commiseration sits at a moderate level of emotional weight. It is not reserved only for the gravest tragedies in life (for those, you would more likely use condolences). Commiseration is perfectly appropriate for everyday disappointments — failing a test, missing a flight, losing a game — as well as for more serious setbacks like a job loss or a difficult personal situation. This makes it a very versatile word.
How It Differs from Similar Words

This is where many learners get confused, so pay careful attention here.

Sympathy is the broadest of these words. It simply means feeling sorry for someone. Commiseration is a type of sympathy — but it is more specific. Commiseration implies an active, expressive sharing of that sorrow. You don't just feel it inside; you show it or voice it to the person.

Empathy goes a step further inward. When you empathise with someone, you don't just feel sorry for them — you actually try to feel what they feel, to put yourself in their exact position. Commiseration doesn't require that level of inner emotional mirroring. It is more about expressing solidarity in sorrow than about perfectly inhabiting another person's emotional experience.

Condolences are specifically reserved for death and bereavement. You would never say "my condolences on failing your driving test." Commiseration, on the other hand, works for any kind of disappointment or misfortune, large or small.

Consolation is about comforting someone — actively trying to make them feel better, perhaps by offering perspective or comfort. Commiseration doesn't try to make things feel better. It simply acknowledges and shares the pain. In fact, sometimes commiseration is more honest and more comforting because it doesn't rush to silver linings.

Commiseration is a warm and dignified word. It carries no negativity. When someone offers you commiseration, it is a kind thing. It signals that the other person is not indifferent to your pain, that they care enough to pause and sit with you in it.

In everyday conversation, people sometimes use it in a mildly informal and even light-hearted way — for instance, friends commiserating together after their team loses a match. But it is also perfectly appropriate in formal contexts, such as a manager offering commiseration to a team after a failed project pitch.

If you had to lock this word into one sentence forever: commiseration is the act of expressing heartfelt sympathy for someone's pain, disappointment, or loss — not to fix it, but simply to acknowledge it and let them know they are not alone in it.
3064: The word commissary has two broad branches of meaning: it can refer to a person delegated to act on behalf of a higher authority, or — more commonly today — to a place where food, supplies, or provisions are stored and distributed. Both branches are in active use, so you need to understand both.
Branch 1: A Person (A Deputy or Delegate)

In its older and more formal sense, a commissary is a person officially appointed to represent or carry out the duties of someone with greater authority — essentially, a stand-in or delegated officer.

Think of it this way: a senior official cannot always be everywhere at once, so they send a commissary — a trusted representative — to handle matters on their behalf in a specific area or for a specific task.

Where you encounter this meaning:

  • In the Church: Historically, a bishop couldn't personally oversee every remote parish. A commissary was an official delegated by the bishop to exercise authority — inspect churches, settle disputes, conduct investigations — in areas the bishop couldn't directly reach. The commissary acted with the bishop's authority but wasn't the bishop himself.
  • In government and law: A commissary could be a government-appointed officer sent to supervise, investigate, or administer something in a region or institution on behalf of the state.
  • In the military: A Commissary General was an officer formally entrusted with the responsibility of procuring and distributing supplies (especially food) to an army. He was acting on behalf of the military command structure to keep the troops fed and provisioned.

The key idea here: the commissary doesn't act for himself — he acts under the authority of someone above him. His power is borrowed, delegated, and defined by whoever appointed him.
Branch 2: A Place (A Supply Store or Food Facility)

This is where the word lives most actively in modern usage. A commissary is a place — a store, shop, or facility — where food and supplies are stocked and made available to a specific, defined group of people.

There are three main contexts where you'll see this:

(a) A Military or Government-Run Supply Store

On military bases and in certain government institutions, a commissary is the official store where military personnel (soldiers, officers, veterans, and their families) can purchase groceries, household goods, and everyday items, typically at prices lower than civilian stores. The U.S. military operates hundreds of these across the country and around the world.

So if a soldier says "I'm heading to the commissary," they mean they're going grocery shopping — but at the subsidized, government-run store on their base, not a regular supermarket. It functions as a benefit: access to this store is part of what military service entitles you to.

The underlying logic connects back to Branch 1: historically, the Commissary General was responsible for feeding the army. The store that grew out of that function — the place where the provisions were actually distributed — inherited the name.

(b) A Prison Store (The "Canteen")

In a prison or jail, the commissary is the in-house store where inmates can purchase items beyond what the prison provides by default: snacks, extra food, toiletries (soap, shampoo, toothpaste), writing materials, stamps, and sometimes clothing like socks or underwear.

Prisoners don't walk up and shop freely like in a supermarket. Instead, they typically place orders from a list and the items are delivered to them, usually once a week. They pay using money deposited into a personal account (called a commissary account) by themselves, family, or friends from outside.

For inmates, the commissary holds enormous importance. The items available there go far beyond comfort — they can represent a small degree of personal choice and dignity in an environment where almost everything is controlled. Certain food items from the commissary become informal currency inside prisons.

(c) A Central Kitchen or Food Production Facility (In the Food Industry)

In the world of restaurants, catering, and food service, a commissary is a large, centrally located kitchen or food preparation facility where food is made in bulk and then distributed to multiple locations.

For example:

  • A food truck operator might not have their own licensed kitchen. Instead, they rent space at a commissary — a commercial kitchen facility — where they do all their cooking, prepping, and cleaning before driving out to serve customers on the street.
  • A catering company that handles multiple events might prepare everything at a central commissary kitchen, then transport the food to each event venue.
  • A chain of restaurants might have a commissary kitchen where sauces, stocks, doughs, and other components are made in large quantities and then shipped out to individual restaurant locations daily.

The commissary here is essentially the "engine room" — unseen by the customer, but the place where the real production happens.

The connection isn't accidental. In both cases, something is being managed and distributed under an organized, structured system of authority:

  • A commissary person distributes authority and carries out official functions on behalf of a superior.
  • A commissary place distributes provisions, supplies, or food to a group that needs them under some organized structure (a military, a prison, a food service operation).

The word always carries a sense of organized supply and delegated function — things being channeled from a central source outward to those who need them.
Which Meaning Will You Encounter Most?

In everyday modern life:

  • If you're reading about military life → commissary = the on-base grocery store.
  • If you're reading about prison life or criminal justice → commissary = the in-prison shop; commissary account = the inmate's spending account.
  • If you're reading about restaurants, food trucks, or catering → commissary = the central preparation kitchen.
  • If you're reading historical, legal, or religious texts → commissary = a delegated official acting on behalf of a superior authority.

ContextWhat "commissary" means
Historical / Church / LawA person appointed to act with delegated authority on behalf of a superior
Military / GovernmentAn on-base store where military personnel buy groceries and supplies at reduced prices
Prison / CorrectionalA store inside a prison where inmates buy food, toiletries, and personal items using funds in their account
Food industry / RestaurantsA central kitchen where food is produced in bulk and distributed to multiple outlets

The core thread across all uses: a commissary is always about organized distribution — of authority, of food, or of goods — to a defined group, through a formal system.
3065: The word commission has several distinct meanings, but they all share a common thread: authority given to someone to do something, or something that results from that authority. Once you see that thread, the meanings become easier to remember.
1. A task or authority officially given to someone

When a person or organization is formally asked — and given the power — to do a specific job, that assignment is called a commission.

The government gave a commission to a group of experts to investigate the cause of the accident.

Here, "commission" means the formal task they were entrusted with. It carries a sense of official permission and responsibility — not just a request, but an authorization.

In art and design, this meaning is very common. When someone pays an artist, architect, or writer to create a specific work for them, they are commissioning that person, and the work itself is called a commission.

The painting was a commission from a wealthy businessman who wanted his portrait done.
She received a commission to compose a symphony for the national orchestra.

The key idea: someone in authority asked for something specific to be made or done, and backed that request with money or power.
2. A group of people officially appointed to do a specific job

A commission can also refer to a committee or body of people formally set up to handle a particular task — usually to investigate, oversee, regulate, or advise.

A commission was set up to look into corruption within the police department.
The European Commission is responsible for proposing new laws for the European Union.
The United Nations Human Rights Commission monitors human rights situations around the world.

These bodies are usually independent, have formal powers, and exist for a clear purpose. They may produce reports, make decisions, or recommend policies.

The difference from a regular committee: a commission is typically more official, often government-related, and usually has a defined, sometimes time-limited, mission.
3. A fee paid for completing a sale or transaction

In business and sales, a commission is a payment — usually a percentage of the sale value — given to the person who made the sale happen.

The real estate agent earned a 3% commission on the sale of the house.
She works on commission, meaning she doesn't get a fixed salary — she earns a percentage of every deal she closes.

This system motivates salespeople to sell more, because the more they sell, the more they earn.

He made a commission of ₹50,000 after selling insurance policies worth ₹10 lakh.

Commission in this sense is essentially a reward for a successful transaction, calculated as a share of its value. It is extremely common in sales, real estate, finance, and recruitment.
4. The act of doing something (usually something wrong)

Less commonly but importantly, "commission" can mean the act of carrying something out — especially a crime or an error.

He was arrested for the commission of fraud.
The law distinguishes between the commission of a crime and the planning of one.

Here, commission is the noun form of "commit." You commit a crime; that act is its commission.

This usage is often paired with the word "omission" (failing to do something). Together, they cover both types of wrongdoing: doing something bad (commission) and failing to do something required (omission).

A doctor can be held liable for both the commission of a harmful act and the omission of a necessary one.
5. A military officer's rank and appointment

In the military, a commission is the formal appointment that makes someone an officer. It is a document — signed by the head of state or a senior authority — that grants a person their rank and authority.

After graduating from the military academy, she received her commission as a second lieutenant.
He holds a commission in the Indian Army.

Someone who has received such an appointment is called a commissioned officer (e.g., a lieutenant, captain, or colonel). This is distinct from a non-commissioned officer (NCO), such as a sergeant, who rose through the ranks without that formal appointment.

Resigning from the military is sometimes described as "giving up one's commission."

On commission
Working in a way where your pay depends on how much you sell, rather than a fixed salary.

All the sales staff work on commission.

In commission
When a ship, weapon, piece of equipment, or system is active, operational, and ready for use.

The new warship was placed in commission after its trials were complete.

Out of commission
When something is not working, broken, or unavailable for use. Used informally for almost anything.

The elevator is out of commission — we'll have to use the stairs.
He's been out of commission for a week after his surgery. (meaning unable to work or function normally)

At the heart of every sense of "commission" is the idea of an act or authority being formally conferred:

  • Meaning 1: A task or authority is given to a person.
  • Meaning 2: Authority is given to a group.
  • Meaning 3: A share of value is given for completing a transaction.
  • Meaning 4: An act is carried out (something is committed).
  • Meaning 5: An official rank and authority is formally granted.

Even "out of commission" fits — something no longer has its active, functioning authority or capacity.

Understanding that core idea — formal authorization or action — will help you recognize and use all these senses correctly in context.
3066:
A committee is a small group of people who are selected from a larger organization or body, and given the responsibility to handle a specific task, make decisions on a particular matter, or look into something — on behalf of that larger group.

The key idea is this: the committee is not the whole group. It is a chosen portion of a larger group, trusted to do a job the whole group cannot conveniently do together.

Think of it this way — a school has hundreds of students and teachers. If there is a decision to be made about organizing the annual sports day, it would be chaotic to involve everyone. So a smaller group — say, five or six people — is picked to plan and decide. That group is the committee.

A committee is not just any random gathering of people. It has three defining features:

1. It is formed with a purpose.
A committee always exists for a reason. It is created to do something specific — investigate a problem, draft a policy, select a winner, manage a budget, plan an event, or review applications. Without a purpose, there is no committee.

2. It is accountable to a larger body.
A committee does not operate independently for its own sake. It works on behalf of a larger organization — a parliament, a company, a school, a club — and usually reports back to it. The larger body gives the committee its authority, and the committee serves that body.

3. Decisions are made collectively.
A committee acts as a group. No single member runs the show unilaterally. Members discuss, deliberate, and usually vote. The outcome represents the group's judgment, not just one person's opinion.

Most committees operate in a fairly structured way:

  • A chairperson (or chair) leads the meetings, guides the discussions, and keeps things on track. This person does not necessarily have more power than others, but they manage the process.
  • A secretary (in many formal committees) takes notes, records decisions, and manages correspondence.
  • Meetings are held regularly (or as needed), where members discuss agenda items and make decisions.
  • Voting is the common method of making decisions. Usually a simple majority is enough — more than half the members must agree.
  • Quorum is a concept you will often encounter with committees. It refers to the minimum number of members who must be present for a meeting to be valid and for decisions to count. If a committee has ten members and the quorum is six, then at least six must be present before any official decision can be made. This prevents a tiny fraction of members from making decisions that affect everyone.
  • Minutes are the official written record of what was discussed and decided in a meeting. Committees are expected to keep minutes so there is a documented trail of their work.

Committees come in several forms depending on how long they last and what they are meant to do.

Standing committee — This is a permanent committee. It exists as a fixed part of an organization and keeps working continuously. For example, a company might have a standing "Ethics Committee" that always exists to review conduct.

Ad hoc committee — This is a temporary committee formed for one specific purpose. Once that job is done, the committee is dissolved. "Ad hoc" itself is a Latin phrase meaning "for this" — formed just for this one thing. For example, a committee formed to organize a charity fundraiser is ad hoc.

Select committee / Special committee — This is typically formed to investigate or examine a particular issue in depth, often in a government or legislative setting. It is usually temporary and ends with a report.

Subcommittee — A smaller group within a committee. When a committee's work is complex, it may break into subcommittees, each handling a different part of the task, before reporting back to the full committee.

Joint committee — A committee made up of members from two different bodies. In governments, for example, a joint committee might include members from both the upper and lower house of parliament.

Committees exist in almost every kind of organized human activity:

  • Governments and parliaments — Legislative committees scrutinize laws, question ministers, and review public spending. (e.g., "The Parliamentary Standing Committee on Finance reviewed the budget.")
  • Companies and corporations — Boards of directors often work through committees. Common ones include the Audit Committee, the Compensation Committee, and the Risk Committee.
  • Schools and universities — Admissions committees decide who gets in. Academic committees set curriculum standards. Disciplinary committees handle violations of rules.
  • Sports organizations — Selection committees pick national teams. Disciplinary committees handle rule violations.
  • Clubs, charities, and community organizations — Almost any club with formal governance will have committees to manage their affairs.
  • Political parties — Committees handle candidate selection, campaign strategy, and party policy.

Outside formal settings, people use "committee" more loosely in conversation to mean any group of people tasked with sorting something out — even without a chairperson, voting procedures, or minutes. You might hear someone say, "We put together a small committee to decide where to go for dinner," simply meaning a few people were chosen to make a call. This usage is casual and figurative, borrowing the spirit of the word.

"Committee" is a collective noun — a single word that refers to a group of people. This creates an interesting grammatical choice:

  • In American English, a committee is treated as a single unit, so it takes a singular verb:
    "The committee has reached a decision."
  • In British English, because the focus is often on the individual members acting together, it can take a plural verb:
    "The committee have reached a decision."

Both are correct in their respective contexts.

When you want to refer to the people on a committee, you call them committee members.

There is a famous saying: "A camel is a horse designed by a committee." This wry expression reflects a criticism that committees, by trying to satisfy everyone and incorporate everyone's input, sometimes produce bloated, awkward, or inefficient results — rather than the clean, sharp solution a single focused person might have produced. This is a real tension in the use of committees: they bring diverse perspectives and collective wisdom, but they can also be slow, prone to compromise, and susceptible to groupthink (where members start thinking alike just to avoid conflict, rather than thinking critically).

This does not mean committees are bad — they are often essential for fairness, representation, and thorough deliberation. But it is a nuance worth understanding.

A committee is a structured, purposeful group of selected people within a larger organization, tasked with handling specific responsibilities on that organization's behalf. It is defined by its collective decision-making, its accountability to the larger body, and its specific mandate. Committees can be permanent or temporary, large or small, formal or informal — but they always represent the idea that some tasks are better handled by a focused, empowered group than by everyone at once or by just one person alone.

To understand "commodification," you first need to understand one smaller word hiding inside it: commodity.

A commodity is something that can be bought and sold in a market — something with a price tag. Oil, wheat, gold, cars, shoes — these are commodities. They have a monetary value, and people trade them.

Commodification, then, is the process of taking something that was not previously bought and sold — something that had a different kind of value, like emotional, spiritual, cultural, or social value — and turning it into a commodity. In other words, it means giving a price tag to something that didn't have one before, and then treating it like any other product in a marketplace.

The key word here is process. Commodification is not a single event; it is something that happens over time, often gradually, as market logic seeps into areas of life where it didn't previously belong.
The Heart of the Concept: Two Kinds of Value

To really understand commodification, you need to know the difference between two types of value:

Use value is what something is actually for — its practical or personal meaning. A song has use value because it moves you emotionally, connects you to a memory, or brings a community together. A glass of water has use value because it keeps you alive.

Exchange value is what something can be sold for in a market — its price in money.

Commodification happens when exchange value starts to overshadow use value — when we stop thinking about what something means and start thinking only about what it can earn. The thing gets reduced to its price, and its deeper meaning gets pushed aside.

This is the soul of the word.

Imagine a village where people fish together in a shared river. Nobody owns the river. Nobody charges for the water. People fish, share meals, and the river is part of community life — it has deep cultural and survival value. Its worth is not measured in money.

Now, a corporation arrives. It buys the rights to the river, builds a bottling plant, and starts selling the water in bottles at a price. Suddenly, something that was freely shared as part of communal life has become a product. It has been commodified.

Notice what changed: the water didn't change. What changed was the relationship people have with it. It moved from being a shared social good to being a tradeable product with a market price.

When something is commodified, several things tend to happen together:

1. It gets a price.
The most visible sign. Something that was priceless — not in the poetic sense, but in the literal sense of having no market price — is suddenly assigned a monetary value.

2. It becomes interchangeable.
Commodities are treated as identical and substitutable. One barrel of crude oil is the same as another. Commodification pushes the same logic onto things that are not naturally interchangeable. For instance, when human labor is commodified, one worker's hour of effort is treated the same as another's — a generic unit to be bought and sold — rather than as the unique skill and effort of a specific human being.

3. Its market value starts to define it.
Once something is commodified, people begin to measure its worth primarily by what it can fetch in the market. Other meanings and values fade into the background.

4. It becomes detached from its original context.
Things that are commodified get stripped of their personal, cultural, or spiritual context and turned into standardized products. A piece of traditional indigenous art, for example, is created within a rich cultural tradition with deep meaning — but once mass-produced and sold as a souvenir, it loses that context and becomes just another item on a shelf.
Examples Across Different Areas of Life

Commodification touches almost every part of modern life. Here's how it shows up:

Human Labor

This is one of the most discussed examples. Before industrial capitalism, most people worked for themselves — farming their own land, making their own goods. Over time, people began selling their time and physical effort to employers in exchange for wages. Labor — the act of a human being doing work — became a commodity to be bought (by employers) and sold (by workers). Your working hours have a price per hour. You are, in a sense, selling yourself in measured units.

Land

In many traditional and indigenous cultures, land was communal and sacred — something no single person could own. The idea of buying or selling land was as strange as buying and selling the sky. But through historical processes (enclosures, colonialism, property law), land was commodified: turned into private property with a market price, to be bought, sold, rented, and speculated on.

Water

As in the village example above, water has increasingly been privatized and commodified. Bottled water is the most obvious example, but so is the sale of water rights to corporations, or the privatization of public water utilities in various countries.

Education

When education is understood as a process of developing curious, thoughtful citizens and human beings, it has a social and humanistic value. When it is primarily treated as a service you purchase to improve your earning potential — a transaction between a student-consumer and a university-business — education is being commodified. The concern is that this shifts what education is for.

Healthcare

In some systems, medical care is treated as a commodity — something you purchase based on your ability to pay, subject to market forces of supply and demand. Critics argue that when healthcare is commodified, the profit motive can conflict with the human goal of healing people.

Relationships and Love

Dating apps present potential romantic partners as profiles to be swiped through, compared, and selected — much like shopping for a product. Some thinkers argue this is commodifying human connection: applying the logic of a marketplace (browse, select, discard, upgrade) to something that was once purely personal and relational.

Culture and Holidays

Many cultural or religious celebrations — Christmas being the most obvious example in the West — have been heavily commodified. What began as spiritual or communal observances have become multi-billion-dollar retail seasons, where the "point" is increasingly defined by buying and selling gifts, decorations, and experiences. The original meaning hasn't disappeared, but market logic has grown to dominate.

Art and Music

An artist creating work as self-expression or community ritual is operating outside the market. But when art is primarily made to sell — designed based on what audiences will pay for, produced for commercial ROI — it enters the logic of commodification. The art still has beauty and worth, but its creation is now governed by market demands.

Nature and the Environment

This is a newer and controversial area. Carbon trading markets, for instance, attempt to assign a price to carbon emissions — and by extension, to the atmosphere's capacity to absorb pollution. Some thinkers argue this is a creative way to protect the environment by giving it economic value. Others argue it is a dangerous commodification of nature itself: turning the air, forests, and oceans into financial assets, which could ultimately make things worse.

Attention

Perhaps the most invisible form of modern commodification: your attention — the time you spend looking at a screen — is collected by social media companies and sold to advertisers. You are not just the user of a platform; you are the product being sold.

The concept is most commonly used in critical discussions — to point out a problem or a concern. Here's why many people find commodification troubling:

It can hollow out meaning. When love, friendship, art, education, or spirituality are treated as things to be bought and sold, their intrinsic meaning risks being stripped away. They become transactions rather than experiences.

It can create inequality of access. If something essential — like water, healthcare, or education — is turned into a commodity, then people who cannot afford to pay are excluded from it. The market distributes things to whoever can pay the most, not to whoever needs them most.

It can cause alienation. Karl Marx, who developed much of the foundational thinking on this concept, argued that when workers sell their labor as a commodity, they become alienated — disconnected from the fruits of their work, from the process of creating things, from other workers, and from their own human potential. Work becomes just a means to earn money, not an expression of skill, creativity, or community.

It can reduce complex things to simple numbers. A school is a living community of teachers, students, and ideas. A price tag cannot capture that. When everything must be quantified and priced, the things that resist quantification — dignity, wisdom, love, joy — get ignored or destroyed.

Not necessarily — and this is important for a complete understanding.

Some economists and thinkers argue that markets and pricing are powerful tools that can make goods more widely available, create efficiency, and even protect things. For example, giving forests a market value (through carbon credits or eco-tourism) might protect them from destruction better than laws alone.

The debate is usually not "all commodification is evil" vs. "all commodification is good," but rather: which things should be governed by market logic, and which things should be kept outside it? Where does the market help, and where does it harm?

There are some domains — basic human dignity, democratic rights, deep personal relationships — where almost everyone agrees market logic is inappropriate. ("You cannot buy a vote." "Friendship cannot be purchased.") And there are areas where commodification seems entirely natural and uncontroversial (buying and selling manufactured goods, for instance). Commodification becomes most contentious in the vast middle ground between those two poles.

Commodification is the process by which something — an idea, a relationship, a natural resource, a cultural practice, a human capacity — that was not previously bought and sold is brought into the marketplace, given a price, and treated as a tradeable product, often at the cost of its original meaning, social role, or human value.

Here's a simple mental anchor: whenever you see the word commodification, ask yourself — "What is being turned into a product here, and what is lost in that transformation?" That question is the heart of the concept. It is about the friction between the world of markets and prices on one side, and the world of meaning, relationships, and human values on the other.
3068:
Before you can understand commodify, you need to understand the word it comes from: commodity.

A commodity is any good or product that can be bought and sold in a market. Think of wheat, crude oil, coffee beans, or gold. These things have a market price. They can be traded. Their value is measured in money. That's it — a commodity is simply a thing with a price tag that you can trade.

To commodify something means to take something and transform it into a product that can be bought and sold — especially something that was not originally meant to be treated as a buyable, sellable good.

In other words, you are turning something into a commodity. You are saying: "This thing now has a price. It can be packaged, marketed, and sold."

Here is the simplest possible version:

To commodify = to treat something as a product to be sold, even if it wasn't meant to be one.

This is where the real meaning lives, and where most learners miss the depth of this word.

Commodifying something doesn't just mean selling it. It means that the act of selling it changes how we think about it. When you commodify something, you are reducing its value to its market price. You are saying its worth can be expressed in money — and nothing else matters more than that.

This is why the word almost always carries a critical or disapproving tone. People use it to point out that something deeply human, sacred, natural, or personal is being treated like just another product on a shelf.

Think about it this way: if a friend helps you move apartments, you thank them, cook them dinner, and feel a bond of friendship. But if you pay them $50 for the same job, the relationship changes — it becomes a transaction. You have, in a small way, commodified their help. The warmth is replaced by commerce.
Real-World Examples (This Is Where It Clicks)

1. Attention
Social media platforms are free to use, but they make money by selling your attention to advertisers. Every second you spend scrolling, your focus is being collected and sold. Critics say these companies have commodified human attention — your mind's focus has become a product.

2. Education
Universities were once thought of as places of knowledge, growth, and intellectual exploration. But when they start behaving like businesses — aggressively marketing degrees, prioritizing profit, treating students as customers — critics say education is being commodified. The degree becomes a product you purchase, not an experience that shapes you.

3. Water
Clean water is something many people believe is a basic human right. When large corporations bottle it, brand it, and sell it at inflated prices — especially in regions where people are desperate for water — people say they are commodifying water. A human need has been turned into a revenue stream.

4. Culture
Imagine a traditional outfit worn for centuries in a specific community, carrying deep spiritual meaning. Now imagine a major fashion brand copying that design, removing all its meaning, and selling it as trendy clothing for profit. That community's culture has been commodified — stripped of its soul and turned into something that makes money for outsiders.

5. Love and Relationships
When dating apps charge you money for features that increase your chances of finding a partner, or when self-help gurus sell you a $299 course on how to be more lovable, some people argue that human connection itself is being commodified. Something that was once purely personal and emotional now has a price.

6. Nature
When forests, rivers, or biodiversity are assigned economic values and traded in markets as "carbon credits" or "ecosystem services," environmentalists often argue that nature is being commodified — the natural world is being reduced to its financial usefulness to humans.

In every example above, notice what is happening:

  1. Something meaningful, personal, or naturally free exists (attention, love, water, culture, education).
  2. Someone finds a way to package, market, and sell it.
  3. In doing so, they reduce its rich meaning to a transaction.

That three-step pattern is the heart of what "commodify" means.
Does It Always Mean Something Bad?

Almost always, yes — at least in how people use the word. The word is chosen precisely because the speaker finds this transformation troubling or wrong.

However, it's worth knowing that not everyone agrees. Some economists and thinkers argue that bringing things into markets can make them more available, more efficiently distributed, and better funded. A pharmaceutical company "commodifying" a medicine, for instance, might be the reason the medicine gets made at all. But even people who accept this tradeoff tend to acknowledge that something is lost when the market takes over.

In everyday speech and writing, if someone uses the word "commodify," they are almost certainly criticizing what is being described.
How to Use It in a Sentence

The verb works like this:

  • "Tech companies commodify personal data."
  • "This trend commodifies grief into a wellness product."
  • "We should not commodify healthcare."
  • "The tourism industry has commodified local traditions."
  • "She argued that modern art has been commodified beyond recognition."

You will also encounter its close relatives constantly:

  • Commodified (adjective/past tense): "a commodified version of spirituality"
  • Commodification (noun): "the commodification of childhood" — this is actually the more commonly seen form in academic and journalistic writing, but it means the same thing: the process or result of commodifying something.

To commodify something is to take something — often something meaningful, personal, or never meant to be sold — and transform it into a buyable, sellable product, typically in a way that strips away its deeper value and reduces it to its price.
3069:
Commodious means spacious and comfortable — having generously enough room for people or things to fit, move, and function with ease.

When you call something commodious, you're saying that it has plenty of space and that the space feels pleasant and practical to be in. It's not just about raw size — it's about space that works in your favor, space that feels like a relief rather than a constraint.
The Key Idea to Lock In

Think of the opposite feeling first: you know that tight, cramped, squeeze-yourself-through feeling of a tiny room, a small car, or an overcrowded cabin? Commodious is the opposite of that. It's the feeling of walking into a room and thinking, "Ah, there's room to breathe here."

So the two ideas bundled together in this one word are:

  • Spaciousness — there is a lot of room
  • Comfort and ease — that room makes life easier and more pleasant

This is important, because learners often mix these up.

  • It does not simply mean big or large. A massive empty factory is big, but you wouldn't call it commodious. The word carries a sense of livable, usable comfort — not just raw scale.
  • It does not mean luxurious. A commodious space can be very plain and simple. A modest farmhouse bedroom can be commodious if it has generous space and you can move around freely. Luxury is about fanciness; commodious is purely about space and ease.
  • It does not mean beautiful. An ugly, bare room can still be commodious.
The Tone and Register of the Word

Commodious is a formal, literary word. You are far more likely to read it than to hear it in everyday conversation. In casual speech, people would naturally say roomy or spacious instead. But in formal writing — travel writing, architecture, literature, real estate descriptions, historical texts — commodious fits perfectly and sounds polished.

If you use it in casual conversation, it will sound slightly elevated or old-fashioned, which is not wrong — just worth knowing.
Sentences That Show It in Action

Reading a word in context is the best way to truly absorb it. Here are examples across different settings:

  • "After years in a cramped studio apartment, moving into the commodious townhouse felt like a luxury." — Here the spaciousness brings relief and comfort.
  • "The ship's captain had a commodious cabin compared to the tiny berths assigned to the sailors." — Relatively speaking, his room was roomy and comfortable.
  • "They chose that SUV specifically because the interior was commodious enough for five adults on a long road trip." — The space made it practical and comfortable for travel.
  • "The old library was surprisingly commodious, with wide reading tables and tall ceilings that made you feel at ease." — Even an old building can be commodious.
  • "The new office layout replaced rows of cramped desks with commodious open workspaces." — The new design allowed movement and ease.
How It Compares to Similar Words

Understanding how a word differs from its close neighbors sharpens your sense of it significantly.

Spacious is the most common synonym and is almost interchangeable. The small difference is that spacious focuses purely on the fact of there being a lot of space, while commodious carries a slightly warmer sense of that space being convenient and comfortable — space that suits you. Commodious is also more formal.

Roomy means the same thing but is casual and everyday. Commodious is roomy's formal, written equivalent.

Capacious focuses on how much something can hold or contain — a capacious bag, a capacious tank. It's about volume and storage capacity. Commodious is about how pleasant and easy a space is to be in — it's a more human, experiential word.

Ample means "more than enough" and can apply to anything — ample time, ample food, ample space. Commodious is specifically about physical space.
What It Is Most Commonly Used To Describe

In practice, you will almost always see commodious used with:

  • Rooms and interiors — a commodious bedroom, living room, kitchen
  • Buildings and homes — a commodious house, apartment, villa, cottage
  • Vehicles — a commodious cabin, carriage, stateroom, SUV
  • Accommodations in general — commodious lodgings, commodious quarters

You would not call an outdoor field or a country commodious — the word works best for enclosed or built spaces that people occupy.
If you ever need to recall this word in a flash: commodious = pleasantly spacious and easy to move around in. It's the word for a space that gives you room to breathe.
3070:
A commodity is a basic, useful good — usually a raw material or a primary product — that can be bought, sold, and traded. Think of things like wheat, gold, crude oil, copper, coffee beans, natural gas, or cotton.

But simply calling it "a basic good" doesn't capture the full picture. The single most important idea behind the word commodity is this: interchangeability. A commodity is something where one unit is exactly as good as another unit of the same type and quality, regardless of who produced it or where it came from.

A barrel of crude oil is a barrel of crude oil. It doesn't matter if it came from Texas or Saudi Arabia — if the grade is the same, you're getting the same thing. Nobody asks, "But whose oil is it?" They only ask, "What is it, and what does it cost?" This is what makes it a commodity. Compare that to, say, a luxury watch. Two watches are not interchangeable in a buyer's mind — the brand, craftsmanship, and origin matter enormously. A watch is not a commodity. Gold is.

Commodities generally fall into a few natural groups:

Agricultural commodities are farm-grown products like wheat, corn, soybeans, sugar, cotton, and coffee. These feed populations and fuel industries worldwide.

Energy commodities include crude oil, natural gas, and coal — the fuels that power economies.

Metal commodities are metals like gold, silver, copper, and platinum — used in industry, electronics, jewellery, and as stores of financial value.

Livestock commodities include cattle and hogs, traded as food sources.

Commodities aren't just bought and sold physically (like at a market or port). They are also traded heavily on financial exchanges — organized marketplaces where buyers and sellers agree on prices. Famous examples include the Chicago Mercantile Exchange and the London Metal Exchange.

On these exchanges, people trade not just the physical goods but also futures contracts — agreements to buy or sell a commodity at a specific price on a future date. For example, an airline might lock in a price for jet fuel six months from now, so they're protected if oil prices rise. A farmer might sell their wheat crop before it's even harvested, securing a guaranteed price. This financial dimension makes commodities deeply important to the global economy.

The price of commodities is determined purely by supply and demand across the world. If a drought destroys wheat crops globally, the price of wheat shoots up. If new oil reserves are discovered, oil prices may fall. No single company or person controls these prices — the market does.

Outside of economics and trade, the word "commodity" is used more broadly in everyday language to mean any valuable or useful resource, even non-physical ones.

For example:

  • "In today's busy world, time is a precious commodity." — Here, time is being called a commodity because it's a limited, valuable resource.
  • "Trust is a rare commodity in politics." — Trust is being described as something valuable but scarce.
  • "Clean water is a commodity that millions of people lack access to."

In these uses, the speaker is borrowing the economic flavour of the word — the idea of something being a resource with real value — and applying it to abstract or everyday things.

This is a subtle but important idea. When people say a product has "become a commodity" or been "commoditized," they mean it has lost its uniqueness and is now competing purely on price, just like raw materials.

Here's a clear example: In the early days of personal computers, a PC was a remarkable, differentiated product. But over decades, PCs became so standardized that all brands offered roughly the same performance for the same price. At that point, most buyers simply chose whoever was cheapest. The PC had become a commodity. Manufacturers lost the ability to charge a premium, because no one product stood out as meaningfully better than another.

This can happen to almost anything — internet services, airline seats, hotel rooms, smartphones in some cases. When the product experience becomes nearly identical across providers, price becomes the only battleground. Businesses generally try very hard not to let their products become commodities, because it destroys profit margins.

A commodity is a basic, interchangeable good — usually a raw material or primary product — that is traded purely based on what it is and what it costs, not on who made it or where it came from. The concept extends into finance (where commodities are traded on global markets), into everyday language (where anything scarce and valuable can be called a commodity), and into business strategy (where "commoditization" signals a loss of competitive edge and uniqueness).
3071:
Common purpose (noun) means a shared goal or aim that a group of people hold together and work toward collectively. It is the idea that multiple people are united not just by being in the same place, but by wanting the same outcome and acting with that outcome in mind.

Think of it this way: when a group of people are not merely together but are together for the same reason — that reason is their common purpose.

The word is built from two everyday ideas:

  • Common here means "shared" or "belonging to all members of a group equally" — not "ordinary."
  • Purpose means a goal, aim, or intention — what you are trying to achieve.

Put together, common purpose = a purpose that is common to everyone in the group — meaning each person in the group holds that same purpose as their own.

In general conversation, you will hear "common purpose" when describing groups — communities, teams, movements, or nations — that are united by a shared objective.

Examples in everyday language:

  • "Despite their differences, the team found a common purpose: winning the championship."
  • "The volunteers were brought together by a common purpose — rebuilding the village after the flood."
  • "A marriage works best when both partners share a common purpose."

Here, the phrase emphasizes unity through shared intention. It suggests that what holds the group together is not just proximity or membership, but a genuine alignment of goals.

An important nuance: having a common purpose is considered deeper and stronger than simply having the same interest or being in the same situation. Two strangers waiting for a bus are in the same situation, but they don't share a common purpose. Two people organizing a protest together do — they are acting with a unified goal in mind.
In Law (The Legal Doctrine of Common Purpose)

In law, common purpose is a significant and precise doctrine in criminal law. It carries serious consequences and is worth understanding clearly.

What it means legally

When two or more people share a common purpose to commit a crime — meaning they have a shared plan or agreement to carry out an unlawful act — and one of them commits another crime during that shared enterprise, all of them can be held criminally liable for that additional crime, even if some of them did not personally commit it, plan it, or even want it to happen.

The key question courts ask is: was that additional crime a foreseeable consequence of carrying out the common purpose?

If the answer is yes, then everyone who was part of the common purpose can be found guilty of the extra crime.

A concrete example

Suppose three people — A, B, and C — plan together to rob a store. That is their common purpose: robbery.

During the robbery, A pulls out a gun and shoots someone, killing them. B and C did not know A had a gun. They did not plan for anyone to die.

Under the doctrine of common purpose, B and C could still be found guilty of murder — because the courts may decide that violence, including potentially fatal violence, was a foreseeable consequence of committing an armed robbery. They joined in a dangerous criminal enterprise, and that act of killing occurred in the course of carrying out their shared plan.

This is a harsh doctrine by design. The law's reasoning is: if you knowingly join a criminal enterprise, you accept responsibility for what that enterprise produces, including acts you did not personally commit.

Why "foreseeability" is the key test

Not every extra crime can be pinned on all members of a group. The doctrine of common purpose does not mean that if you plan to do crime X with someone, you are automatically guilty of every crime they ever commit. The extra crime must have been reasonably foreseeable as something that might happen in the course of carrying out the shared plan.

  • Joining a plan to commit a violent robbery → violence during the robbery is foreseeable → you bear liability.
  • Joining a plan to commit a nonviolent fraud → your co-conspirator separately murders someone on an unrelated matter → that was not foreseeable from the fraud plan → you likely do not bear liability for the murder.

Where this doctrine applies

The doctrine of common purpose is used in criminal law systems in the United Kingdom, South Africa, Canada, Australia, India, and many other countries. The exact rules and requirements vary by country, but the core idea — shared criminal plan = shared criminal liability for foreseeable outcomes — is consistent across these systems.

In some places, this doctrine is also called "joint enterprise" or "acting in concert." These terms describe the same essential principle.
The Common Thread Between Both Uses

Whether in everyday language or in law, the phrase "common purpose" always carries the same essential weight: when people share a purpose, they are bound together by it. In ordinary life, that binding is motivational and moral — it unites them. In law, that binding is legal and consequential — it makes them jointly responsible.

ContextMeaning

In everyday English, common purpose is a shared goal or aim that unites a group of people, giving them a collective direction and driving their joint action.

In criminal law, common purpose is a doctrine that holds all members of a group liable for crimes committed by any one of them during the execution of a shared unlawful plan, provided the crime committed was a reasonably foreseeable consequence of that plan.

In both cases, the concept carries a strong message: to share a purpose with others is not a passive thing — it creates real bonds, real responsibilities, and real consequences.
3072:
"Common sense" means basic, practical judgment that helps you navigate everyday life without needing special training, a textbook, or an expert's advice. It's the mental ability to look at an ordinary situation and just know what the right or reasonable thing to do is.

Examples:

  • You know not to touch a flame because it will burn you.
  • You know to save some money for emergencies.
  • You know that if you insult someone, they'll likely be upset.

Nobody formally taught you these things in a classroom. You learned them through experience, observation, and basic reasoning. That's common sense at work.

The phrase has a surprisingly rich history. It comes from the Latin term "sensus communis," which the ancient Greek philosopher Aristotle used around 350 BCE. Back then, he wasn't talking about practical wisdom the way we mean it today. He was talking about something more technical: the idea that humans have five separate senses (sight, hearing, smell, taste, touch), and the brain needs one central faculty that gathers all that information together and makes sense of it as a whole. He called this unifying faculty the "common sense" — the sense that is common to all the senses.

Over centuries, the meaning gradually shifted. By the time of the Enlightenment (roughly the 1600s–1700s), "common sense" had evolved to mean something very close to what we mean today: the ordinary, reasonable judgment that every sane, normal person supposedly possesses.

The Scottish philosopher Thomas Reid made this idea famous in the 18th century. He argued that certain basic truths — like the fact that the physical world is real, or that our memories are generally reliable — are not things we need to prove with complicated arguments. They are simply obvious to any healthy, rational human mind. He called this body of self-evident knowledge "common sense" and built an entire school of philosophy around it, called Scottish Common Sense Philosophy. His point was: stop overthinking the basics. Some things are just plainly, obviously true to any reasonable person.

Then in 1776, the American founding-era writer Thomas Paine published one of the most famous political pamphlets in history, titled Common Sense, in which he argued that it was simply obvious — requiring no deep political theory — that the American colonies should be free from British rule. He was using the word to mean: "This is so clearly right that any ordinary, reasonable person can see it."

To really understand the term, it helps to look at each word separately.

"Common" here does not mean low-quality, ordinary in a negative sense, or dull. It means shared by everyone — as in, something belonging to the community, accessible to all. Like a "common area" in an apartment building is shared by all residents. So "common sense" is the sense, or judgment, that is common to all human beings — the basic reasoning ability we all share.

"Sense" here doesn't mean the five physical senses. It means judgment, understanding, or mental perception — the way we use it when we say "that makes no sense" or "she has a good sense of how things work."

Put them together: common sense = the shared judgment that all people are naturally expected to have.

Common sense has several key features:

1. It's practical, not theoretical.
Common sense deals with the real world in front of you, not abstract ideas. A philosopher might debate whether you can truly know that fire is hot. A person with common sense just doesn't put their hand in the fire. Common sense is about doing the right thing in real situations, not analyzing them academically.

2. It's learned from experience and observation.
Nobody is born with common sense fully formed. It develops as you grow up, watch the world around you, make mistakes, and observe cause and effect. A toddler doesn't know that a wet floor is slippery and dangerous. An adult does — because either they've slipped before, or they've seen others slip, or they've been told about it. This experience-based learning, when internalized and applied automatically, becomes common sense.

3. It's fast and intuitive.
Common sense operates quickly. You don't stop and calculate when someone drops something — you instinctively reach out to catch it.
