Two people from the same village are not compatriots — they are neighbors, or locals. Two people from the same country are compatriots, even if one is from the north and the other is from the south.
The Tone and Register of the Word

"Compatriot" is a slightly formal word. You would not typically hear it in casual, everyday conversation. Instead, you are more likely to encounter it in:

  • News and journalism — "The minister met with her compatriots abroad."
  • Sports commentary — "He was supported throughout the tournament by his compatriots."
  • Political speeches — A leader addressing citizens might say, "My dear compatriots..."
  • Formal or literary writing — Authors use it when they want precision and a slightly elevated tone.

In informal speech, people usually say things like "a fellow Indian" or "another American" instead of "compatriot." But in writing and formal contexts, "compatriot" is both natural and widely used.

Here is a key thing to understand: the relationship that "compatriot" describes is purely factual. It is not warm by definition, and it is not cold by definition. It is neutral — a statement of shared national identity, nothing more.

However, the context in which people use the word often carries warmth. When a crowd cheers for "their compatriot," there is pride involved. When a leader addresses "dear compatriots," there is a sense of unity. The word allows emotional warmth, but it does not guarantee it.

Compatriot vs. Fellow citizen
"Fellow citizen" emphasizes the legal or civic bond — you both hold citizenship in the same country. "Compatriot" is slightly broader and more about national or cultural origin. For example, if someone emigrated from India to Canada and gave up Indian citizenship, you might still call them a compatriot (they are from India), but calling them a "fellow citizen" of India would no longer be accurate.

Compatriot vs. Countryman / Countrywoman
These words mean almost exactly the same thing. "Countryman" and "countrywoman" are older and slightly more informal or old-fashioned. "Compatriot" is gender-neutral, which makes it the more common and versatile choice in modern usage.

• "The two scientists were compatriots — both from Germany — but they had never met before the conference."
  • "Living abroad made her appreciate her compatriots more than she ever had at home."
  • "The rescue team searched for survivors, paying special attention to their compatriots trapped in the building."
  • "He felt an instant connection with the stranger when he learned they were compatriots."

If you ever need to recall this word quickly:

A compatriot is simply someone who comes from the same country as you (or as the person being discussed) — nothing more, nothing less.
3099:
To compel means to force someone to do something in a way that leaves them no real choice.

The force doesn't have to be physical. In fact, most of the time it isn't. It can come from a law, a situation, an emotion, a moral obligation, or even a powerful inner feeling. What makes it "compel" and not just "ask" or "urge" is that the pressure is so strong that the person being compelled feels they cannot reasonably say no — or genuinely cannot refuse at all.

The most common way "compel" is used:

compel + someone + to + do something

  • The judge compelled the witness to testify.
  • Hunger compelled the man to steal bread.
  • His conscience compelled him to tell the truth.

In each case, something or someone is applying a force — and because of that force, the person has to act. They aren't choosing freely. They are being pushed or driven into action.
Two Main Situations Where "Compel" Is Used

1. When an outside force makes someone act

This can be a person with authority, a law, or a circumstance.

  • The law compels citizens to file taxes.
  • The emergency compelled the doctors to work through the night.
  • Her boss compelled her to sign the document.

Here, the source of the compelling is external — something outside the person is applying the pressure.

2. When an internal force makes someone act

This is very common and very important to understand. Feelings, emotions, morals, and inner convictions can compel just as powerfully as laws or authority figures.

  • Guilt compelled him to apologize.
  • Curiosity compelled her to open the letter.
  • Love compelled him to stay.

The person isn't being physically held or legally required to do anything. But the internal pressure is so overwhelming that they feel they have no real choice.
"Feel Compelled To" — A Very Common Phrase

One of the most frequent ways you'll see "compel" used is in the phrase "feel compelled to do something."

This means: you feel such a strong inner pull toward doing something that you almost can't stop yourself.

  • I felt compelled to speak up when I saw the injustice.
  • She felt compelled to call him, even though she knew she shouldn't.
  • He felt compelled to warn them about the danger.

Notice: nobody is forcing these people from the outside. But the feeling inside is so powerful — duty, conscience, emotion, urgency — that doing nothing feels impossible. This is the psychological depth of the word.

You'll often see "compel" used in the passive voice:

be compelled to + do something

  • The soldiers were compelled to retreat.
  • She was compelled to accept the terms.
  • Citizens are compelled to obey the law.

This passive construction emphasizes the person who is being forced, rather than the thing doing the forcing.
What Makes "Compel" Different from Similar Words

Understanding what sets "compel" apart from nearby words will sharpen your understanding considerably.

Compel vs. Urge
When you urge someone to do something, you strongly encourage them — but they can still say no without major consequences. Urging is a push; compelling removes the real option to refuse. Urging leaves choice intact. Compelling nearly eliminates it.

Compel vs. Force
These are very close in meaning and often interchangeable. But "force" is more commonly associated with direct physical pressure or brute power. "Compel" is broader — it can include emotional pressure, circumstance, logic, or authority. You would naturally say "the evidence compels us to conclude" — but saying "the evidence forces us to conclude" feels a bit rougher. "Compel" is more versatile and works in both formal and emotional contexts.

Compel vs. Coerce
Both mean to make someone do something against their will. But "coerce" carries a darker shade — it usually implies threats, intimidation, or manipulation. If someone coerces you, it often means they used fear or harm to get compliance. "Compel" can be completely neutral (a storm compels you to stay indoors) or even positive (love compels kindness). "Coerce" is almost always negative and implies a wrongful use of pressure.

Compel vs. Oblige
"Oblige" means to make someone do something, often because of a duty, rule, or social expectation. It is slightly softer and more polite in tone — "I am obliged to inform you." "Compel" is stronger, sharper, and carries more urgency or force. You would say "the court compelled him to testify" (strong legal force) but "politeness obliged her to respond" (social duty, softer pressure).

This is the soul of the word. Whenever you see "compel," ask yourself: Is there genuine freedom here, or has the force made a free choice nearly impossible?

  • A crying child compels a parent to respond. Can the parent ignore the child? Technically yes — but the emotional pull is so strong that most people would say they had no real choice.
  • A law compels you to stop at a red light. You could run it, but the legal consequence removes the real freedom to choose otherwise.
  • A guilty conscience compels a person to confess. They could stay silent — but the inner moral weight makes silence feel unbearable.

In all these cases, "compel" captures the idea that something has reduced or removed free will — either from the outside (authority, law, force) or the inside (emotion, conscience, overwhelming feeling).

To compel = to force someone to do something, leaving them no real choice.

The force can be:

  • External: a law, a person with power, a threatening circumstance
  • Internal: a strong emotion, a guilty conscience, a moral conviction, an overwhelming feeling

The key idea is always the near-absence of real choice. The person is driven, pushed, or pressured into action — not freely choosing it.
